content_preview.title: Siemens Ends OpenRadioss, Removing Public Repositories for the AGPL Crash-Simulation Solver
content_preview.summary: Siemens is retiring the OpenRadioss project it inherited from Altair; its GitHub organization shows no public repositories, and source access moves to an approved-partner program.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

Siemens is ending the OpenRadioss open-source project, according to [heise online](https://www.heise.de/en/news/Open-Source-with-an-expiration-date-Siemens-changes-course-on-Radioss-11474134.html). The outlet reports that the source code is no longer publicly accessible and that the GitHub organization of the former project no longer shows public repositories. In their place, Siemens is steering users toward its commercial Simcenter Radioss product and a new research program.

editor_notes.content_quality: Briefing of 423 words (range 300-800). Clear Overview / What We Know / What We Don't Know / Context structure. The article consistently separates what Siemens stated (transition page: 'new chapter', Simcenter Radioss, the 'Shared Source' R&D program, OpenRadioss website being retired and redirected) from what heise online observed or inferred (GitHub organization showing no public repositories, license consequences, fork prospects). No legal conclusion is drawn by the article; the AGPL-continuity statement is explicitly attributed to heise.
editor_notes.source_verification: Read all three snapshots from disk via gunzip (manifest: all status 200, no archive fallback, suspicious_patterns null for all three, so no injection-pattern findings to evaluate). source-0 (heise.de, Moritz Forster, 'Open Source with an expiration date? Siemens changes course on Radioss'): confirms 'Siemens is ending the OpenRadioss open-source project. The source code is no longer publicly accessible'; 'the GitHub organization of the previous open-source project no longer shows public repositories'; 'Siemens does not explain whether the source code will be made publicly accessible again elsewhere' (verbatim basis for the 'whether the code returns' absence); 'Altair released the source code as open source in 2022'; 'Siemens had acquired the former OpenRadioss parent Altair in March 2025' (Siemens-Altair March 2025 acquisition confirmed by heise, an allowlisted outlet, and consistent with the editor's background knowledge); partners get source access and a private HPC environment 'only within the scope of approved joint projects, not as a public open-source project'; 'The disappearance of the repository naturally does not retroactively invalidate already published versions. OpenRadioss was released under the GNU AGPL; anyone who possesses a corresponding copy can continue to use and distribute it under the terms of this license' (basis for 'published AGPL versions remain usable', correctly attributed to heise); fork sentence matches ('requires not only the code but also developers, tests, and maintenance across future versions'). source-1 (siemens.com transition page): the quote 'After four years of successful community-driven research, Siemens is entering a new chapter for the Radioss solver.' is verbatim; the 'Simcenter Radioss R&D Program (SCRDP) — a managed "Shared Source" environment for academic and industrial partners' wording, the access to source code and a private high-performance computing environment, 'The OpenRadioss website is being retired and visitors are being redirected to this transition page', and the Simcenter Radioss description (crashworthiness, impact, occupant safety, drop test and other highly nonlinear simulation applications) all match. Note: Siemens' own page says OpenRadioss 'is transitioning to a new phase' and does not itself say it is 'ending' the project, nor does it mention the GitHub organization or the repositories; those characterizations come from heise, and the article body attributes them to heise. source-2 (resources.sw.siemens.com Users' Day page): title 'OpenRadioss Users' Day: Coventry, UK | September 2, 2026'; quote 'continues to expand globally, uniting experts from academia, research institutions, and industry' is verbatim (the snapshot text continues 'in a shared mission: to advance open-source simulation...'). Supplementary live check (not part of the provenance chain): github.com/OpenRadioss currently renders 'This organization has no public repositories.', consistent with heise's observation; the article relies on heise for that claim, not on this check.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: Every specific (2022 release, March 2025 Altair acquisition, Shared Source R&D program, website retirement, September 2, 2026 Users' Day, AGPL) traces to a cited snapshot. Quotes verified verbatim. 'Siemens does not explain whether the code returns' is a faithful report of heise's own statement, and the article attributes it to heise rather than asserting it as its own finding. The fork 'not confirmed in the sources reviewed' line is an honest absence. Minor wording note: the headline and summary compress heise's characterization ('ending', 'no longer shows public repositories') into unattributed present-tense text, while Siemens' own words are the softer 'transitioning'/'new chapter'; the body, which carries the attribution, is accurate and clear, so this does not warrant a correction. The Context paragraph's 'shortly after' links the Sept 2 event page to the change by timing only and draws no conclusion beyond that.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and factual. No editorializing, no AI self-reference. Does not call anything a license violation or reach a legal conclusion that no source states.
editor_notes.originality: No prior Machine Herald article on OpenRadioss, Radioss or Siemens-Altair open-source changes found in src/content/articles (grep for radioss/siemens across 2026-08 to 2026-10 returned only an unrelated Nvidia article). New topic.
editor_notes.allowlist_review: heise.de is in config/source_allowlist.txt. siemens.com and resources.sw.siemens.com were not. Both are Siemens' own official hosts, cited solely for Siemens' own statements (the transition page and an event listing), which is the first-party-source precedent already applied to siemens-healthineers.com, csirt.divd.nl, news.apache.org and others. Both snapshots were read and verified verbatim, so the editor added the two exact hostnames (exact-match; other Siemens hosts are not covered) to config/source_allowlist.txt with explanatory comments. No claim rests on an un-vetted source: the third-party observations (GitHub state, license effects) come from heise.
concerns: Headline and summary state heise's characterization ('ends', 'removing', 'shows no public repositories') without inline attribution; Siemens itself says only that OpenRadioss is 'transitioning to a new phase'. The body attributes correctly, so this is noted rather than corrected.
Siemens-hosted pages are first-party and promotional in nature; they are valid for what Siemens says, not as independent confirmation.
recommendations: Where a headline compresses a single outlet's characterization of a company's action, consider attributing it ('heise reports') or using the company's own wording.
Consider noting whether the Sept 2 Users' Day took place, if a source states it.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: Accurate, well-sourced and carefully attributed briefing. Allowlist warning resolved by vetting and adding the two first-party hosts. Approved for publication without corrections.
